newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Uzbeks raid West for grain with Russian bins empty.
newsitem.headline: Uzbeks raid West for grain with Russian bins empty.

text.p: Uzbekistan will import up to 1.2 million tonnes of wheat this year, an official grain source said on Wednesday, as the Central Asian state conceded defeat with its harvest and despair that Russia had little to sell.

The Uzbek source, who did not want to be named, said Uzbekistan would begin buying bread-making wheat on European markets this month, mainly through U.S. grain trader Cargill and Glencore AG of Switzerland.
The source, who reported Uzbekistan imported around 1.6 million tonnes of grains in 1996, said the country would also buy wheat from the United States and Kazakhstan.
"With the rise in food prices, the population in recent years has consumed more bread as the cheapest product," he said.
"Uzbekistan will for the next few years make purchases on the world market as the quality of much of its own wheat does not meet food standards."
The import news followed months of market talk in European grain centres that the former Soviet republic might be a grain buyer after harvests across the former Soviet Union failed.
The Uzbek source said that Russia, a traditional supplier, would not export much wheat this year on account of its own poor harvest.

Andrei Sizov of Russian independent agricultural consultancy SovEcon Ltd said Tashkent's hopes of bartering large amounts of cotton for Russian grain had fallen through, and that only small transactions would be carried out.
The Uzbek government said last December that it had agreed with a Russian textile firm to exchange cotton fibre for 400,000 tonnes of Russian grain.
One grains source said that a proposal that Russia import Argentinian wheat to carry out the barter deal had fallen apart.
"I think it will be difficult for the Russians to fulfil the (barter) contract," the Uzbek source said.
Uzbekistan harvested 2.7 million tonnes of grain in 1996, according to the latest official figures, up from 2.4 million tonnes in 1995.
But even 1996's improved output was far short of the estimated 4.0-4.5 million tonnes of food wheat needed to feed Uzbekistan's 23 million people.
The Uzbek source said that private commodities trader Cargill sold the country 913,000 tonnes of food wheat in last year, delivered via Estonia, to make up for the shortfall.
Uzbekistan's strongman president and former Communist Party boss, Islam Karimov, two years ago called for a Soviet-style plan to make the largely-desert nation self-sufficient in grain.
But diplomats and grain traders in the secretive republic have for several months predicted that Uzbekistan would have to import over a million tonnes of wheat to feed its population.
They say that over one third of the country's marginal land is not irrigated, while Soviet-era canals are unlined and uncovered, leading to a huge waste of valuable water.
